newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile's El Abra sees stockpiles lasting to mid-Nov.
newsitem.headline: Chile's El Abra sees stockpiles lasting to mid-Nov.

text.p: El Abra copper mine can keep up production with its stockpiles into early or mid-November while workers dig out the mine's stricken conveyor belt, the mine's site manager John Fenn said.
Fenn said production at the open pit mine in northern Chile remained halted but that the rest of the mine's production areas, including heapleaching, was going ahead with stockpiles, he said.
"The mine is stopped because the ore is carried by the belt," he told Reuters by telephone from the mine.
Asked if stockpiles would last to early or mid-November, he said, "Yes, that's correct."
A key conveyor belt carrying copper ore from the mine to a crusher plant was buried under tonnes of debris on October 9 when a tunnel collapsed on it. Four workers died in the accident.
Fenn said it was unclear when the belt would be working again but that "it's a manageable problem."
"We are excavating the belt and we are ordering parts so we'll have them on hand to repair the belt," said Michael Rounds, spokesman for the mine's owners Cyprus Amax.
The mine made its first cathode in August but is expected to reach full production of about 225,000 tonnes of copper a year in the first half of 1997.
Officials have said that although the mine was still in "startup mode" when the mishap occurred, they don't expect it to delay the mine's timetable for coming fully onstream.

Rounds countered charges of lax safety practices by one of El Abra's contractors by saying that the project's accident rate is actually well below those of both the Chilean and U.S. construction industries in general.
Company figures show an accident rate of 0.8 during 17.5 million work hours to end-August, compared to an average 1.6 in the United States last year and 8.0 in Chile, he said.
"This means our accident rate was actually 10 times as good as that of Chile in general," he said from Cyprus Amax headquarters in Englewood, Colorado.

"By saying this, we don't want to minimize the importance of what's happened but we have a good safety record and we consider safety a priority," he said. El Abra had discussed safety codes "very extensively" with contractors in the past, he said.
The head of Chile's top mining safety regulatory board on Thursday publicly accused the tunnel's builders, which he identified as Parina Limitada, of cutting corners on safety.
